content.rendered:
Greg Wilkes (00:02):

So today’s podcast stems from a recent coaching course that I was actually on. I was just over in Hawaii on an intensive training program. And the whole point of that program was to make my coaching experience better for my clients. And there was a subject that we discussed there that I thought was actually really transferrable over into the construction industry and that was onboarding clients. So what we were learning at this event was the importance of onboarding clients the right way. If you get clients signed up to your program and then they have a terrible experience in the first 30 days while you’re trying to onboard them or you overwhelm them or different things like that, then it’s highly likely they’ll either not enjoy the program altogether ’cause you’ve started off on a bad foot or they’re gonna leave your program because they haven’t enjoyed the onboarding experience.

 

 

(00:51):

So I thought to myself, well how does this actually relate to construction? And interestingly enough, there is, uh, a big crossover actually, and we do have to also think about how we onboard clients. And a lot of the time this isn’t really focused on at all in the construction industry. So what is client onboarding? Well, what we’re talking about here is we’re talking about the period between when a client initially signs up for you. So they’ve signed a contract and they’re willing to go ahead with the project and then the period of when you actually start on site. So there’s a gap in between those two areas. And this is the perfect time to actually give the client an onboarding experience where you set out the expectations of how you want themselves to act during the process and what the relationship’s gonna be like. You are gonna give them your criteria of how you are gonna act and you might give them timelines and some other things that are going on so they’ve got a full picture of of what’s going on.

 

 

(01:52):

So the reason we’re focusing on onboarding is because I see it all the time where clients potentially stop the process after the sale has ended. So what they seem to think is that once we’ve won the sale and we’ve secured a deposit and it’s in the bank, I don’t have to worry about the client experience so much now ’cause we’ve, we’ve nailed the process. We’ve, we’ve got them in the bag and that’s the end goal for many construction companies. But really that’s just the beginning of the process. Winning the sale isn’t the end at all. And it’s really important that, especially if you’ve got a sales team, that we make that transition from the sale to the start of the project as smooth as possible to keep the client happy all the way through. And if we can enhance the client’s experience after the sale, then oftentimes they can be raving about us. Before we’ve even started the project, I’ll just give you an example for how my company used to do it. One thing we did is when we signed a client up, we would immediately go and send them a hamper just to say thank you. So it’d be a welcome hamper, maybe some champagne or chocolates or cheese or whatever it was. And that welcome hamper went over with a a gift card. And we would just say, we’re so excited to work with you. Thanks for signing up with us. We are really looking forward to delivering your project. We can’t wait for you to get to know some of the team over the coming months. Just a, a simple hamper like that. And it went over as soon as we’d signed someone up. So we had no obligation to do that in the onboarding process. That wasn’t the only thing we did, but that was one of the things. But you wouldn’t believe how many times we would then get recommended from clients just because we’d done something like that. So all of a sudden we’d get a phone call in and they’d say, oh, you’ve just been recommended. You are about to start a project for my friend over the road.

 

 

(03:40):

And they, they said that we have to talk to you as, uh, our builders because you’ve given ’em such a great experience already. And we think we haven’t even done anything for ’em yet. All we’ve done is sign them up and sent them a a hamper worth 50 pounds. So it’s amazing what the little things can do to keep your customers happy. So we wanna talk about that, how we can really enhance that experience. And it’s more than just giving hampers. There’s, there’s a lot more involved. Now, one of the dangers of not giving a client a very nice experience, and let’s imagine the experiences a client’s just signed up with a big project for you. They’ve potentially put their life savings into it and they’ve signed on the dotted line and you’ve got that deposit payment into the bank. You send them a receipt saying, yeah, payment received, and then that is it.

 

 

(04:28):

You go completely quiet. And let’s imagine their project doesn’t start for another eight weeks or 12 weeks. And that could be likely sometimes ’cause they might need planning permission or they might need to, you know, to get permits approved or whatever it’s gonna be. Now if you went completely cold in that period of time, what do you think’s going on in the client’s mind? They’ve never had work done like this before, have they? And think about what they’re hearing in the media. Always hearing about cowboy builders running off of their money, unscrupulous firms, you know, spending the deposit and then going bust. They’re gonna have all these things and these worries going on in their head. And then on top of that, we’ve then got all the worry that’s coming in from the media. So they’re looking at interest rates rising. They’re worried about are they gonna get the value back on their property?

 

 

(05:17):

’cause their property prices are potentially plunging. They’re seeing material prices go up, uh, they hear about their friend over the road who had a contract done and the the builder put in extra costs at the end ’cause he wasn’t making enough money. So all these things are potentially going on after a client has signed with you and they’re now rethinking their decision. Was it the right thing for me to do this or not? I know I’ve just give given this company a 10 grand deposit, but actually do I really want to go ahead with this project now? And sometimes, and this can happen, quite often a client regrets the decision they’ve made and they may want to pull it back in and they may say, listen Greg, I’ve actually decided I don’t wanna go ahead with this project now. Can I have my deposit back because we are in some financial difficulties or my mortgage has been pulled or whatever it’s, they say, and they may try and get out of the contracts that you’ve initially signed.

 

 

(06:21):

Now, most contracts, I know, you know, people listening to this, listening from the UK and maybe the US and other parts of the world, not saying it for everyone, but generally there’s a 14 day cooling off period on many contracts and you may have to give that deposit back in full. Other times you may not give the full deposit back, but you won’t necessarily be able to keep it all and you may have to give some of that deposit back. But the, the more important thing, it’s not about the deposit, is it, it’s about potentially you’ve lost a huge contract, you know, you could have had a 500 K or million contract and that’s gone. It doesn’t matter what deposit you’ve potentially got, all that profit is gone if a client decides it’s not right for them at this time. But a good onboarding process, if they’ve got a great experience and they feel like the project’s already begun right after they’ve signed the contract, it makes it much harder for them not only to get out of contract, but it just feels like the project’s going and it gives them less opportunity to start rethinking their decision.

 

 

(07:22):

So that’s why it’s absolutely crucial that we’ve got a really good experience for them after they’ve signed. Now we’ve, we’ve already discussed thinking about what’s going on in the client’s head and we wanna reassure them over some of these things that are in our control. So some things that are in our control, we obviously we can’t control interest rates and we can’t control property prices and whatever else. But there are other worries that we’ll be going through our client’s mind that we can control and put them in ease with. And they’re gonna be worried about potentially delays on the project. They’re gonna be worried about you going over budget and it costing them more. They might be worried about the quality of workmanship, all those things. These are genuine worries from a client and you may have dealt with some of this in the actual initial sale, but now you may just have to reassure them again when you are onboarding them.

 

 

(08:13):

So there could be little things you can do just to, to put them at ease. Maybe if they’re worried about delays, you could send them your project timeline and your Gantt chart. Make sure that’s nice and detailed for them so they can see, yeah, this is all mapped out. I know when it’s starting, I know it’s when it’s gonna finish. If they’re, uh, potentially worried about the budget increasing, maybe you could put their mind at ease by ordering some materials in advance and locking in some prices. If they’ve got some big ticket items like kitchens or bathrooms or other big ticket items that you’ve gotta put advanced orders on, can you secure them during that period so that the client can be assured that the the price isn’t gonna go up as the project goes on. So these are the sort of things that you can do.

 

 

(08:57):

Maybe if they’re worried about the quality, you can show them your quality control documents. Have you got documents in place that when you sign off a particular item of work, for example, when you’re signing off the roof, you might have a quality control checklist and you could show the client that and say, just to reassure you, we’ve got this in place and these are the sort of things that we are gonna be monitoring during your build. So like I say, you may have covered some of that off in the sales process, but if you haven’t, this is a chance for the customer just to get you to know you a little bit more, a little bit more about of your process. And it just puts their mind at ease that they’ve picked the right person, they’ve made the right choice. And what we want to do as a construction company is just really try and empathize with that client.

 

 

(09:41):

We, we know in our heads that some of these emotions and some of these things they’re worried about might be completely irrational and not relevant at all and we know how we do things in the background, but just remember your client doesn’t, oftentimes they’ve had no experience in this whatsoever. They’ve never had a big project done, so this is completely new to them. So we just wanna really empathize with them and understand their concerns and address those as needed. So how do you design a effective onboarding process? Well, we really wanna think about what steps it takes in order to get to the actual start of the project. So there may be a few things that we just wanna list out initially of how long it’s gonna take from when we sign a contract to actually starting on site. And you are gonna have an internal process that you go through that you really want to list down.

 

 

(10:34):

So some of that process might start with, right, we’ve gotta get our permits in place before we start work. We’ve gotta get the site set up, we’ve got to order materials, we’ve got to have a pre-start meeting with the client. We’ve gotta discuss communication channels, we’ve gotta get them set up on software that we’re gonna communicate over and and track. So there, there’s gonna be a load of things that you do in the background and sometimes you might do this without your client even knowing, but it’d be really good if you listed out those steps and just advise the client of what those steps are. So even if you’re not necessarily including them in those steps, you could just send them a quick email and just say, right week one, just want to let you know what’s happening. We are going to be applying for this permit and that permit and we’ll let you know once that’s approved.

 

 

(11:19):

Week two we’re doing this, week three we’re doing that. And if we can give them a little bit of a, a program or an outline of how the onboarding process works, that can really put their mind at ease and they just know exactly what to expect going forward. You’re just keeping them in the loop throughout. One thing we found was really useful was having a pre-start meeting with a client to run through all of this. So we would, we would get on site, we would sit there with the client and actually at this meeting we would have the sales person at the meeting and we’d also have the project manager at the meeting we thought was, it was quite important to have both of them there together just in case something was said at the, on the sales call that the project manager didn’t understand and, and hasn’t interpreted.

 

 

(12:02):

So we would make sure there was a clear and easy transition between the sales side and the project management side. And during this pre-start meeting, again, we’d be running through things like, how long are things gonna take, what’s the timeline going to look like? Um, what materials or what things does the client need to source? They may have to make decisions about, as we said before, what type of kitchen they’re gonna have or bathroom or whatever else. So you wanna try and nail all that early on before the build even starts to get them making decisions because it’s gonna make the build a lot easier and it keeps the ball rolling While you are waiting to start on site. You might wanna set the communication channels. How are you gonna communicate? Is it gonna be via email? Is it gonna be by something like Slack?

 

 

(12:45):

Is it gonna be by WhatsApp? I highly encourage it not to be by WhatsApp for your project manager’s sake, because you know, there’s nothing worse than that phone going off all night to to deal with clients unless you’ve got like a separate, separate phone that you’re gonna be able to deal with that. So think about all those things. Talk about the roles and responsibility of, of every member. The client has also got responsibilities. The architect may have responsibilities. So talk about those roles, get it nice and clear because your client isn’t gonna understand who’s got to do what. They may be expecting you to do everything, but some of the responsibility might be down to someone else. So it’s really important to, in that pre-start meeting, to get them to understand who’s doing what on the project, if possible. Can you use a project management app to keep your clients feeling in the loop?

 

 

(13:31):

There’s some great apps out there like build a trend. We’ve got a personal app that we use that we’ve developed called Cost tracker. Can your clients be involved in that? Can they see what stages you’re at? And on a lot of these apps, if they’re good ones, you can actually show your clients certain things but not other things. So you want to establish with the client how the, how the commun communication channels are gonna be and what project management tools you’re gonna use. Get them set up on all of that and make sure they understand it all so that they’re ready to go. Another thing we can do during this pre-start meeting is really manage the client expectations. Because sometimes, and you’ve probably experienced it, clients can have completely unrealistic expectations about what’s gonna happen. So you’ve probably seen it all the time where you tell a client, right, this is a 12-week project, it’s worth a hundred k and then all of a sudden the client adds another a hundred K worth of extras, but they still expect the project done to be done in 12 weeks.

 

 

(14:27):

And you think, you know, what you talking about is that’s not realistic, but how much easier it is to have that conversation before you even start. So set those expectations and be realistic with a client about how it goes. So we can say to the client, look, we’ve got this project scope and schedule, this is what it’s gonna look like if we stick to that. But if you change your mind on anything we need to know in advance, and that may impact the schedule, it may increase the time, it may change the way our project schedule looks, it’s obviously gonna increase the cost. And then let them know how you are gonna send costs over variation orders and change orders. How do you send them, how should they be approved? Should they be signed? How they shouldn’t just be verbally giving orders to people on site.

 

 

(15:13):

You’ll have a communication channel of how you want extras and variations communicated back to you as a company. So all these expectations need to be managed. Um, the client may have in mind the way they want to do it, but it needs to fit in with the way you do it as a business. So if you outline exactly how you want that process to look, it makes things a lot easier. One thing we used to do was ensure that a client understood the boundaries of when they could contact their project managers or site foreman. So we would say to a client that the site manager or foreman is working from eight till 5:00 PM that’s the time that you can get hold of that person and at 5:00 PM they go home and they’re with their family. So they’re not gonna be responding to texts or emails at seven, eight o’clock at night.

 

 

(16:01):

However, if there’s an emergency, this is the number you call, or if there is an emergency, you do this and give your process of what they need to do in that situation. So set those boundaries, it’s really important. Set those boundaries at the pre-start meeting. Otherwise you will get clients texting you at 10 o’clock at night expecting a reply. You may also have a complaints procedure or an escalation when things are not going too well. So we can tell the client that, look, if you’re unhappy with something, the first thing you need to do, rather than them contacting the MD straight away or the c e o, you could say, this is what we do. You first make your concern known to the project manager or the the site foreman, he will then escalate it to the project manager. The project manager. If if he can’t deal with it, it can then be escalated to the MD or C E O.

 

 

(16:53):

So we wanna have a clear process in place for complaints and how we deal with things when the client isn’t happy. And again, it’s important to outline that to the client. Otherwise every single problem they may try and bypass your management team and come and talk to you directly as the C E O and clearly you don’t want that happening. One other thing I’m a big believer in is also communicating bad news to clients as soon as you need to. And sometimes we can really hold back delivering bad news to clients because we think, oh, you know, I’d rather just try and deal with this myself or I’ll see if there’s another way around it or they may not find out. So we’ll sweep that under the rug and not tell ’em about that. But communicating bad news is so important because it establishes trust straight away.

 

 

(17:40):

If we can be straight with a client and say, look, I’m sorry but this has happened. But also rather than just delivering bad news, we also deliver them what solution we are looking to implement. So yeah, we’re really sorry this permit didn’t get applied for. We’ve got a two week delay, whatever it is. But what we’re gonna do with this two week delay, we are gonna apply these extra resources and we’re gonna get that two weeks back halfway through the build, whatever it’s, we’re gonna say, it’s just an example. So don’t be afraid to deliver bad news to a client. And on the onboarding process, you may tell them that, you may let them know that, look, if we’re running behind or something happens, we are gonna be straight up with you and be completely honest all the way through. And we expect that honesty back in return.

 

 

(18:22):

Clients respond to that, they like that and it builds trust and integrity. So there’s some of the points that you might wanna think about with your onboarding a lot there that we could potentially cover. But the principle that you want to really get in your mind is that if you are gonna onboard a client, what we want to do is make sure that that process in between signing a contract to actually deliver an on site, something is going on. And that onboarding process might be regular emails that go out. They might be actual pre-start meetings that you have with a client. You might be telling the client how you set up their sites and giving them progress that way. But whatever you do, you need to design your own onboarding process that works for you and the business and you need to then communicate that back to the client, give the client the best experience they can possibly have before you even start works on site. And it’s gonna gain you more referrals, it’s gonna give you a great reputation and it’s really gonna enhance the customer experience. So I hope that helps a little bit. If you’d like some more tips on how we can help you grow your business and put some systems and processes in place so you can have a great experience for you as the business owner and the client, then reach out to us in our developed mastermind. We’d love to show you what we do.

title.rendered: Are Coaches a Waste of Time Transcript

content.rendered:
Greg Wilkes:

 

So, I’m coming at you with this episode all the way from Hawaii. I’m over here. You might be thinking what you’re doing over in Hawaii. Well, it’s not holiday. I’m just here for six days and I’m here to be coached myself. I’ve actually got a business coach who helps me scale my business. And what I wanted this podcast to be about is why I feel a business coach is vital for anyone who’s trying to grow themselves personally and grow their business. I’m gonna tell you a little bit about my journey. We’re gonna talk about why you might need a coach and why some have resistance towards getting coaching. We’ll talk about some of the benefits of investing in the right training courses. We’re also gonna talk about what happens if a coach or a training course is not working the way you want it to be, and how you can be a good student if you are gonna invest in this sort of time, um, and resource to improve yourself.

 

 

So, let’s jump into it. First of all, let me just tell you a little bit about why I’ve got a coach. So obviously I’m a construction business coach, but originally I was a builder. So I’ve come from, uh, carpentry backgrounds, did an apprenticeship. You’ve probably heard my story before. Grew quite a big company and I know how to grow businesses. That’s one thing I can do really well. But there’s a difference between knowing how to do something and, and writing down the theory, and then being able to teach that to others. Because if you don’t learn the right method of teaching, what you can do is you can have potentially great content, but then no one can implement it because you’re not actually teaching or training it the right way. So there’s definitely a different skill set needed from being a coach to being just a good business person.

 

So it is really important to me, even though I wrote my book and I was getting great feedback from the book that yeah, your ideas are fantastic and they’re working for us in the business, uh, it was really important for me that we actually had to make that really practical for people to be able to, to do that. So I was hungry to grow my coaching business and I didn’t really know all the strategies in order to do that. I knew how to get construction clients, but how would I go and get clients that potentially wanted to be coached and how would I structure my program and what would I teach? What niche would I go for? Would I go for people that are on the tools or people that have established businesses and things like that? So there was a lot of decisions to make.

 

So I researched coaches left, right, and center on who would be the best at this. And I’m a massive believer in picking someone who’s in the best in the industry for what they do. And I found a, an amazing coach. His name is Tacky Moore. He’s based out in Australia, and I eventually started with him. I was really small at the time, only had a few one-to-one clients when I started with him back in, oh, when was it now? March I think, 2021. When sort, I sort of really started kicking things off. Since I’ve been with this coach, I’ve actually 10 xd the size of my business, which is absolutely incredible. So the 10 x is just brilliant, not just for me personally, ’cause obviously it’s financially better for me, <laugh> if I 10 x the business, but I’m having more of an impact on the world.

 

I’m having an impact in my coaching clients’ lives. They’re able to impact their own lives and, you know, have more time, freedom and money for them and their families. So it’s a massive reward for me, uh, to see other people get results. But it’s also, you know, a great lifestyle for me. And because of the coaching, I’ve been able to move over to Sydney, Australia. I can still run my coaching business from there. I’ve got clients around the world that are in my program, and really I’m able to create a, a business that’s timeless and spaceless because I’ve got recorded videos that people can watch. They can watch that anytime of the day. And spaceless, I can literally do this anywhere in the world, hence why I’m recording this episode from Hawaii. So me having a coach personally has completely transformed my business. I do believe I could have grown a business successfully without having a coach, but what he’s done is sped it up without a doubt.

 

I’ve definitely managed to get there a hell of a lot faster than that, than I would’ve done on my own. And it’s also helped me grow as a person because I’m listening to other people in the group program. I’m, uh, mixing with other world class coaches and I’m seeing how they do things differently. How they don’t allow the coaching business to overtake their lives. How they, you know, don’t allow clients problems to, uh, completely take over their lives. ’cause it can do, sometimes you’re not just a coach, but you feel like a, a psychologist and a counselor sometimes. And, and fair enough, because people have problems from business that really impacts their own personal lives and their marriages and all sorts. So it is really been valuable to, to be with people in that space that understand what I’m going through. And it’s obviously a completely different ball game to construction.

 

So enough about me and why coaching’s benefited me. I wanna talk about why you should invest in your personal self-development and your business. And one of the big reasons is because construction is changing. The construction industry is a little bit of a dinosaur, and sometimes it takes ages to actually change, but we are seeing huge changes in this landscape. The first change is coming from our marketing, the way we market ourselves, the way we now have to be on social media. Uh, we have to have a, a good website. You have to be out there, you have to be doing videos and vlogs and whatever else. And sometimes people can get left behind if they’re not actually doing any of these things and they’re just relying on word of mouth and recommendations. You can really get left behind in the construction industry. So you have to evolve with it.

 

And if you’re not comfortable in doing things like that, then that’s why you potentially need to invest in self development so you can learn how to market yourself as a business. So that’s, that’s one of the, the first reasons also, we’re seeing a big change with AI at the moment, that’s gonna be completely transformative for construction. And if we wanna stay ahead of the game, we need to understand how to use AI in our business, whether that’s in our marketing on our social media, whether that’s using it to help us with our operations, our contracts, our job descriptions for staff. There’s tons of reasons why we might use ai. And clearly if we’re not using that and our rivals are, we are gonna be left behind. So self-development and investing in training programs that teach you how to use AI is absolutely key. So you can evolve, evolve with the industry.

 

We’ve always got new software that’s arrive in, so there’s project management tools, tools to manage your finances. We wanna be on top of the latest, uh, technology for these tools, how to price jobs quickly and efficiently. And if we have an understanding of what software is out there, then obviously we’re gonna save a huge amount of time. And if we’re in a course that shows us what all those tools are and the best ones to use for us, then that’s gonna be a real game changer too. We also wanna improve our own skills and abilities. So if you’re anything like me, you know, I did okay at school, not fantastic, but I was trained to be a carpenter. The only official qualification I have is to be a carpenter and, and an electrician actually. So, so I’ve got two official qualifications there, but none of those qualifications taught me about business.

 

Not at all. They didn’t tell me <laugh>, how to understand the profit and loss report, how to hire, how to fire, all, all those sort of things. You, you don’t get taught any of that during your carpentry trade. So there’s so many in construction that are now running businesses and they might have a few people working for them, but they’ve never, ever been taught or learned the skills and have the ability to, to run an effective to construction company. And they may be running it okay at the moment, at whatever size they are. Maybe they’re at 500,000 or a million, but are they gonna be able to run a 2, 3, 4, 5 million pound company or more? So when you invest in that self-development, you are learning how to improve your skills and abilities and your, your investing in yourself really to, for your future. The other reason for investing in self-development is because you are clearly wanting to grow the business and improve your own prosperity in life.

 

And if, uh, self-development, uh, can get you there, if you can upskill yourself and you learn new things and it means you can take on better projects and better contracts and earn more money, then of course you’re gonna wanna invest in that self-development in yourself so that you’ve got the ability to do that. So we know the reasons why people invest in training and self-development is quite obvious, isn’t it? But what is coaching? What’s the difference between coaching and maybe just training? So first of all, what a coach is there for. Just like if we give an example of someone who may play sport, you may get one of the best tennis players in the world, let’s say Roger Federer, I know he’s retired now, or <inaudible> or someone like that. Uh, an amazing tennis player, literally the best in the world. And then you think, well, why have they got a coach?

 

Why on earth would that person need a coach? Well, the reason is, is because when they’re doing their thing and they’re in their flow, that tennis player can’t see where he’s going wrong. He can’t see that he’s changed his grip on his racket, and that’s making him hit the net more than he should. He can’t see that when he’s serving, he’s losing power in his serve because of the ball toss or something like that. So even though they may be fantastic at what they do the best in the world, who are interested in improving, always invest in coaches. So we understand what a coach does and that obviously a coach can motivate someone, they can help out with their mindset. If they’re not feeling right, they can, you know, talk to about about why that is and really get to the depth of the, the matter and help ’em overcome that.

 

So a good coach will be able to do that for you. But it’s different than just investing in training. So training is where you are learning how to do something. You’re being educated on a particular subject, but a coach is the one that can help you implement it and they can show you the strategy on, alright, now you understand how to do this, but how are we gonna be able to implement this for you and your, uh, construction business? And that’s really the difference between a coach. A good coach will hold you accountable. So if you commit to doing something in a week and say, yeah, I’m gonna get that done, a good coach will just give you a little tap on the back and say, Greg, how did you get on with that? You promised you were gonna send your profit loss report over.

Did you manage to do it well, Greg, you said you were gonna invest in that training software, have you managed to do it? So a coach can hold you accountable, he can help you with your skillset and really they can see things that you can’t see. So that’s really what a coach is. But there’s again, there’s different types of coaches, there’s so many coaches out there, and then you need to think, well, what is the right type of coach for me? So you get some coaches that are just generic business coaches. They may have created a, a brilliant business in the past so they know the principles of business itself. And yeah, business is based on principles and those principles are sometimes universal, but it’s also good to get a coach who’s specific in what you are looking for. So for me personally, I’ve got a coach who I believe is one of the best coaches of coaches, <laugh>, that’s all he does.

 

So he just coaches other coaches and his whole training program is around that. So it’s perfect for me. I’m not learning something, I don’t need to know it at this time. So if you’re gonna invest in a coach as a construction business, you wanna find a coach that fits your criteria. Are they a construction coach? Have they been there and done what you’ve, are their skills transferable to your business? So rather than getting a generic coach, you want to get, try and get someone if you can, that understands you and the industry and that’s gonna be a huge benefit. There are of course benefits from other coaches. Don’t get me wrong. I’ve also had other coaches that aren’t as specific to, to train me in other areas. So I had a coach who was training me on how to grow my different social media channels.

 

I had a coach that helped me with my podcast. So not saying you only ever have one coach that’s, that’s just for construction, but you need to pick the right coach at the right time and and make sure that they’re gonna be able to help you grow in the specific area that you are looking at. So that’s the different types of coaching and, and what coaches there are. But really the, the point I probably want to try and get across is I can’t tell you the value in me personally having a coach. What a difference it’s made in my business. Picking the right coach has been instrumental and I’ve had other coaches before and they haven’t been right, but when you find the right one, it can really be a game changer. And this coach, I’ve got no intention of of going anywhere because he’s gonna take me to, uh, my goal, which is to ultimately help 10,000 construction business owners create more time, freedom and money.

And I really believe that coach is gonna get me there. So we understand coaching, let’s just talk about the reasons why people may resist getting a coach altogether or, or or getting trained in what they’re doing. So there’s a few myths about coaching and training that, or misconceptions you could say that exist out there. Some of those misconceptions. And what, what people sometimes feel is that the coach is gonna do everything for you. So they feel they can come and get a coach, tell ’em all their problems, and then their coach is just gonna magically fix their business. And that just doesn’t happen. That’s, that’s not reality. You may get some done for you coaches that can do elements of your business, but there’s gonna be no coach out there that’s gonna take your business over for you. So the reality is, if you wanna grow and you want to improve, then you are gonna have to do the work.

 

And a coach is just gonna point you in the right direction and give you the training to help you do it. So he’s gonna upskill you, give you the skillset to do it, and then point you in the right direction of how to do it or, or potentially point you in the direction of someone that can help you do it, but the coach isn’t gonna fix your business for you. So you’ve got, um, be prepared to, uh, deal with that. Another reason people worry about getting coaches is because they’re worried about changing. They feel that a coach may completely change how their business looks at the moment and may suggest to them things that they just don’t want to do. And they worry about what impact that’s gonna have on their business. Or what if they tell me to fire this person or do that, or what if they ask me to do something that really puts me outta my comfort zone.

 

So that fear of change can hold people back and I understand that. And one thing we’ve gotta in mind is that a good coach should be able to understand what you can and can’t do. And at the end of the day, it’s your business. So while me personally as a coach, I’m pretty honest with my clients. If I don’t feel they’re doing the right thing, I’ll tell ’em straight. But if there’s massive resistance to doing something because it doesn’t fit their personality or their life, then a good coach needs to find another way of implementing a different strategy in order for it to work for their client. ’cause at the end of the day, you just want your clients to win. And it doesn’t mean that you are always right all the time. Sometimes you need to adjust it. So some people resist coaching because of, of a little bit of a, a fear of change.

 

Others resist because they’re worried about the financial concern. When you invest in a coach, generally speaking, you’ve got maybe a a 12 24, 36 month program. You know, you don’t turn a business around overnight. It’s a long process. You know, some, some people with coaches their entire lives because they’re creating, you know, huge companies. So people worry about that financial commitment, am I gonna be able to afford it? And the reality is a lot of people come into coaching because the fin, they’re financially struggling in business and it’s sometimes when that financial hit happens and they’ve got that financial pressure, then they start thinking, oh, last, last resort I’ve gotta go and get a coach. And it’s, that’s really too late <laugh> at that point. And that’s not the time to become into coaching when you are financially distressed because you can’t turn businesses around overnight. It takes time to implement strategies and then time to see the results of that.

 

Well, I always call it, there’s a little bit of lag before between when you do something and when you actually start seeing the results from it. So financially, if you’re worried about getting into coaching, I think you really need to plan that. You’ve got, you know, I dunno, a three to six month budget to, to cover the coaching then hopefully the, the coaching itself should be able to pay for itself. If it didn’t pay for itself, then it wouldn’t be a good coaching course. But you hope that the impact of the coach in helping you get more leads and more projects is gonna be able to pay for itself anyway. So that, that should address the financial concern. There are obviously huge benefits with working with coaches. I mean, I’ve got a ton of case studies from my clients. Uh, one of my favorite case studies is probably a client that come to me.

 

His name was Dominic, who’s, uh, with me in the program at the moment. He’s been with me a couple of years I’d say. And he initially come to me because he was approaching retirement and he’d always had amazing projects. He was always doing well, got great leads and got good projects on board. But he had a few years of really bad financial, uh, really bad sort of financial decisions that were made. And he wasn’t making the money he should in this business. He couldn’t quite work out why, but he had a few years of a loss. So he had some years he was doing amazing then obviously a few years of a loss. And as he was approaching retirement, he thought, wait a minute, I’m not gonna be able to pay my mortgage off here if I carry on at this rate and you know what’s going on.

 

I’m working really hard, I’m getting amazing jobs, but haven’t got any money to show for it. In fact, I’m actually losing money may as well see at home and just write a check out to your clients. So what was going wrong? So we uh, really done a deep dive into what was happening in Dominic’s business. We immediately got him on what we call our profit and loss tracker. So we start analyzing his profit every single month. We did him a forecast of what we wanted to get him to, and then we measured his strategy every single month. If there was a month he didn’t hit, we’d have to dive into why. And then we’d look at those specific projects. He started tracking not just his monthly profit and loss, but each individual project. So we could then dive in and say, well, why is this project not coming in on budget?

 

What’s gone wrong? Was it the pricing? Has it run over time? What is it that’s done it? And by having all these figures to hand and having all this data, it’s really easy for a good coach to be able to analyze that and come up with a, a solution based on that data. So because we had that data going forward over the course of that year, Dominic went from being a company that was losing money to making over 300,000 pounds in profit, which was absolutely incredible. What was even more special though about this was that the next year he went on a cruise around, I’m sure it was the Caribbean or The Bahamas, something like that. And he had just a satellite phone. So he left his phone at home. He had no signal, had a satellite phone for emergencies, and was able to leave his business for two weeks because he’d put the right systems and process in place for it to run without him.

 

So that’s probably, you know, one of my favorite case studies because it massively impacted his financial situation, but it was impacting his life. He now had absolute confidence that he was gonna pay off his mortgage and he was getting some more time back to enjoy his business and his life by, by being able to go sail him. And there’s loads of case studies like that and that’s, that’s what what’s amazing. If you look on my website, you’ll see case studies of all sorts of people that have had massive success in the industry because they’ve invested in a coach or some training. You also see people personally growing, which I think is fantastic. You see people coming out of their shell a little bit and growing as a person. You see some people, they come on some of our coaching calls and they’re really shy and quite introverted.

 

And then as they start building their confidence and their skills and uh, the way they’re running their business, they, they, you know, they become really alive on the calls and that feeds through into the way they pitch to clients. So now when they’re pitching to clients for sales, you see their confidence coming through and their ability. So they’re winning better contracts ’cause clients are buying into them too. So we see massive personal growth with people also, which is really encouraging and and heartwarming for me to see. And obviously if we manage to impact the business, which means their employees are happier and if we manage to impact the business, it also means we’re impacting their lives, their personal lives. ’cause these people have all got families, wives and potentially kids to go home to. And if their business is going well and they’re not stressed out and they’re earning good money, then of course life gets better.

 

You know, you get to take your kids to Disney and uh, you get to have a Friday off and take your partner out for lunch and you get to take your kids to school or go to their school play. You can do all of that if your business is running the right way. So, huge benefits personally and in business by investing in a coach. So how do you choose the right coach? How do you choose the right training program? Well, we touched on this before. I think it’s really important to get someone who’s industry specific, but also you wanna get someone who’s dealing with what your problem is at the moment. So is your problem that you haven’t got a right, the right plan in place? Maybe you don’t know where you’re going and you’re just winging it a little bit and you haven’t really got a, you know, a one or five year plan of how you’re gonna get there.

 

You dunno when it’s the right time to hire that next project manager or bring on, uh, a social media market or whatever. It’s you need, there’s just no plan there. So if it’s plan that you need, you need to find a business coach that can help you with that plan is it may be that you need to attract better clients to your business. You’re sick of working for the clients that are always, um, struggling with money and they’re run outta money at the end of the project. Maybe you want to attract more affluent clients, maybe you wanna attract bigger projects. So if that’s the case, you need to find a client, a, a, a coach who is excellent in attracting more leads to your business. That’s really important. Maybe it’s that you can’t convert, maybe you’re not very good at the sales side of it.

 

So you get tons of leads through the door and you’re pricing all these projects up, but you’re not winning any of them or, or winning a really low amount. You’re sick of spending money, um, and time pricing all these jobs up and not winning them. So maybe you need a coach that can help you with your conversion or maybe it’s that you need a coach that can help you with the delivery side. Yeah, you might have a load of work you might be able to convert, but <laugh> the delivery on site could be a mess. You know, you’re very disorganized, people are always waiting for materials. Your jobs are always overrunning. Maybe your health and safety shocking on site or people aren’t doing what they should be doing or the qualities going downhill. So there could be some real problems with delivery and maybe you need a coach that can help you with the actual delivery side of things.

 

Or it could be still on delivery. It could be the back office. You could have, you know, your sites may be running really well, but maybe your back office is a mess. Paperwork everywhere. You’re not on top of your numbers, haven’t got any software installed. So you know, the, the office is just chaotic and, and stressful. So a a, a business coach that’s good at systems and procedures and operations that could be perfect for you. Or maybe you’re at a size now where you are ready to scale and you wanna scale fast to the next level. Maybe you’re already a business at one to 3 million, you wanna get to five to 10 and you are looking for someone, a coach that can help you with hiring the right sort of people, getting the right company culture in place, how you can measure and manage as a business owner so you can step back.

 

Maybe it’s that type of thing that you need. So you really need to decide what type of coach you want and is there a coach that can fit all those or tick all those boxes? And you’re never gonna get a perfect coach out there. You know, it’s rare to find someone who’s the best at what they do across all the areas. But if there’s someone that you think can cover all those bases or is, you know, highly good at one specific thing that you wanna resolve, then that’s the sort of coach that you wanna be looking for. When you are going with a coach, you could always ask if there’s a trial session, you know, are you able to test out the program before you have to commit? ’cause most coaching programs, as we said, the 12, 24 36 months or the, you know, ongoing, you, you probably wanna just check if there is a coach that can, you know, do like a four week trial just to see if you like it or not.

 

One thing we offer is what we call a love it or leave it offer because we believe in the first 30 days, you know exactly whether or not it’s gonna work for you. And if it’s not right for for us and it’s not right for you, then you know, clearly you’re probably better off not being in the program because we don’t wanna work with people that are not happy in the program and, and, uh, are not doing well. And likewise, you’re not gonna wanna be in the program if you, if you don’t think it’s right. So try and find someone who potentially gives you a little bit of a trial period if, if possible. So let’s imagine you’ve taken the step, you realize that coaching is right for you, uh, you can see the benefits, but now you want to know is it working or not?

 

You know, how do I know if this is working for me? Am I running at the right pace of everyone else? Well, one way to measure that is by ensuring that you set key performance indicators or KPIs right at the beginning of your journey. You wanna understand the metrics that lead to progress or that indicate progress. So maybe one of your metrics is, I’m currently a million pound a year company and I want to hit 2 million pounds for this year. Let’s imagine you wanna double, so what are gonna be the metrics that measure that success? Yeah, of course you could just look at the end of the year and go, yeah, I’ve hit 2 million, but how much better it be if actually there was a, a real plan in place of how you get from one to 2 million? How much should I invoice in January?

 

How much should I invoice in February? How do we get that growth spur and are there gonna be quiet periods in my calendar? Maybe if you’re a little bit seasonal like a plumber or a gas heating engineer, you may be really busy in winter, but then the summer dies down. So you wanna understand and set the right KPIs. In that instance, if it was, you know, financial revenue that you’re going for, maybe it’s not that, maybe it’s profitability or maybe you wanna measure how many staff you’re taking on or how many teams you’re bringing on board, but whatever you’re doing, you have to set KPIs right at the beginning of your journey so you understand what it means to make success. And if you are hitting those KPIs, you know you’re on the right path. So that’s really important. Maybe you’ve got other things you wanna do there, maybe it’s personal growth that you’re looking for.

 

So you might personally be thinking, well I want to, I want to have more time as a person to, you know, grow myself and grow my mindset and read more books and things like that. So sometimes a coaching program can help you with that and they can, you know, show you how to get some more time back so you can do those things and maybe in the group that you’re in, they talk about books they’re reading all the time and that can inspire you. So that can be a bit of an indicator of progress if you are reading those books and then implementing them. So you’re seeing personal growth and of course you wanna see business growth across all areas of the business as we, we’ve spoken about the financial side of it, but you also wanna see it with your employees. You know, are they coming along for the journey?

 

Are they happy there? Are they enjoying it? Are they making progress? Are they stepping up to, uh, more management positions because they see a, a future with you as a company? So all of that can give you indicators that coaching and training is working for you. But what about if it’s not working? What’s a sign of a a coach that’s just not working for you? Well, one thing we always look out for is what we call red flags in a business. And we specifically measure our red flags with re in, uh, with regard to revenue, first of all, so sorry, not just revenue, but revenue, uh, gross profit, net profit, all those things. We track all those KPIs. If we see a business owner getting red flags consistently in one area, let’s imagine that their gross profit is dropping every single month and they’re not hitting their KPIs, then we’ll need to get that business owner on a call and just have a chat go, right, Greg, what’s happening?

 

You, you turnover’s fantastic. You, you’re getting more work than you ever have before, but why are we not making as much money on these projects? What’s going wrong on the project delivery side? And then we’d have to do a bit of a deep dive into why that is. Is it that they’re spending too much on materials? Is it that their labor costs have shot up? Are they underpricing work? So we’d have to dive into what those things are, but seeing many red flags and, and, and those red flags not being dealt with is an indication that the coaching is not working. A red flag is, is great in a way because it, it, it just puts a marker there. And then, you know, a good coaching program will dive in immediately and say, right, let’s address this. But if there’s consistent reg flags happening all the time, then something’s not right there and it’s not being, not being dealt with.

 

Um, if a coaching program doesn’t seem to be working for you, then you really need to find a solution and work out why is it that the communication style’s not right? Is it, uh, the way that you’re being trained isn’t right? So hopefully in your trial period, you’ve already be been able to establish if the the style of coaching is right for you. But if something’s changed in your personal life and things aren’t just working the way they were before, then you need to really try and find a solution with that. So talk to your coach and see if there’s a way of you getting yourself reset again and back on track. And, and sometimes you just need to accept reality. You know, if you come to an end of a coaching program and it just hasn’t been right, maybe your styles haven’t worked well together and you’re just a bit of a personality clash or you don’t enjoy the group that you’re in, then you know, the reality is if it’s not working for you, you might need to move on and find another coach or another program that is gonna be a little bit more suited.

 

But how can you ensure that a coaching program is gonna work? How can you be a really good student when you’re being coached? Well, one thing we always emphasize is being a really good listener and getting involved in the group training side of the program. ’cause in our masterminds, we’re a big believer in that there’s more power in many brains than just one. And we know that those that are regular on our group coaching calls, uh, can make massive progress because they’re listening all the time to what’s going on in other people’s business. So they might come on and talk about their own stuff, but then in the backgrounds maybe they’re, they’re just working away in the background, but they’re listening to what other people are going through and the problems they’re having and, and then the solutions that they’re finding. And that’s really key.

 

You’ve gotta listen attentively and really focus in on the training so you’re understanding the nuances of it to, in order to apply it into your business. Of course, listening is important, but there’s no point just listening. You need to actively implement what you are learning. So really important to understand the training. And once you’ve understood that training, you’ve processed it in your mind, you then need to go out and implement that strategy and put it into play. There’s no good having it all up there as theory. You’ve actually gotta implement it and, and see it take, take fruit and take action. And then probably the, the third area of being a good student, I would say is you’ve gotta be open to receiving honest feedback. It’s no good having a coach that just tells you, you’re doing amazing all the time. <laugh>, sometimes you need someone that’s gonna be constructive and say, listen Greg, it’s amazing what you’re doing here, but can I just tell you one thing that I can see is just not working?

 

These social media posts you’re putting out are just not right at the moment or your website isn’t looking right or your presentations that you’re sending to clients, you’re just missing this. And you’ve gotta be open to that feedback that’s so important that you accept that it’s not a slight on you and your personality, it’s just, you know, open and honest feedback on, on how you can improve and you’re investing in yourself. You’re here for improvement. So be open and be willing to accept that. So we’ve covered a lot here just, uh, recapping some of the stuff we’ve looked, we’ve looked at why I got into coaching, how it 10 x my business. We’ve talked about why you should invest in self-development and and and what a coach is, um, why you might resist coaching, the benefits of of working with a coach and how you can find the right training program, what to do if a program isn’t working for you, and how you can be a good student too.

 

So lots of lots of stuff we’ve covered there. If I was gonna say one thing though, I would say that a good business coach is worth their weight in gold. If a coach can help you speed up the, the time it takes you to grow. So, alright, you might, if you’re at 1 million, you wanna get to 2 million, yeah, you’re probably gonna get there anyway on your own if you are that sort of person. But if a business coach can help you do it in half the time or you can help you do it without making some of the mistakes that you might have made along the way, or you can be upskilled in a certain area so you’re improving the business and you’re improving your life, then of course a business coach is gonna be worth it and it’s worth that financial investment in yourself and in your business. So I hope that epi episode helps a little bit. If you ever wanna talk about potentially coming into our program and being coached by me, we’d love to be able to talk to you if you qualify for that. But I wish you all the best and speak to you on the next episode.

Harnessing Hidden Talent: The Case for Internal Hiring Transcript

content.rendered:
Greg: [00:00:00] So if you are listening to this and it’s May 2023, then you are just in time to potentially book your ticket to our live in-person event in West London on the 30th of June, 2023. It’s be an absolutely incredible event, and I’d love it if you could come. We’re going to be looking at your marketing, your sales.

We’re going to be coming up with strategies on how we can take your business from one to 5 million pounds if you’re looking to scale. And also we’ve got some confirmed top guest speakers that are going to be attending. So you’ll can find out more about it on our website. I’ll put the show note links at the end of this podcast.

But grab yourself a ticket. It’s a great event to network and meet some other like-minded business owners that are just like you, hungry to grow their construction businesses. Let’s jump into the podcast.

Greg: [00:01:00] So today let’s talk about the subject of promoting from within. Now, we always talk about how there’s a lack of skilled trades, and particularly it gets even more difficult when you’re looking for skilled management. We might be be talking about site foremans, buyers, contracts, managers, project managers.

Once you start moving up the management chain, the lack of skillset becomes even more apparent, and it can be really difficult when you’re trying to expand your business, when you know you need to hire people like this or where to look. So today I just want to try and talk about is there potentially that talent pool from within your own company?

Because we often overlook members of our staff for these positions, but actually it could be the best thing you could do is to try and look from within and promote from within, if you can. But there might be a few things that hold you back from doing that. And initially the reason why you might not promote is the first thing that might frustrate you or hold you back is that you worry about their skillset and their lack of experience in the role.

[00:02:00] So maybe you’ve had someone with you a long time. You’re looking to promote them as a project manager, and you think, do you know what? I’m just not sure if they’re going to be up to it. Are they good enough on technology and emails? Have they got the organidation skills to do this role? And these are valid concerns because you don’t want to promote someone who’s clearly not got the skillset just because they’ve been with you a long time and they’ve been loyal to you, clearly they’ve got to be able to fulfill the higher role.

But there are ways of overcoming this sort of thing. One of the things you can do if you’re worried about that lack of skill and lack of experience is really come up with a training plan, a comprehensive training plan for that employee and see if a bit of mentoring, a bit of coaching, and you encourage that continuous learning.

[00:03:00] That could be what gets that employee over the line and upskills them. Think about practical ways of doing that. Can you start initially just testing that employee with extra responsibility? Maybe you want them to do a takeoff on site and say, “right, I want you to measure the materials in this room or the materials on the drawing for a certain part or a certain phase of the project, and send it over to me.”

Then you could check that and make sure that they’ve done the takeoff right. You could let them go and source quotes for the materials potentially. “Right, here are three suppliers. I want you to phone them all, source quotes, get the best quote and put the order in.” Maybe you let them set up the site organization for the day, so at eight o’clock in the morning, they’re briefing the site team about what they want done.

It might be great if you’re off for the day or you know you’re ill, or you’ve gone on holiday. This could be a perfect time to test them out for this and just see are they able to manage a site potentially and organize a day’s work for the site teams? These could be specific ways that you could just let someone off the leash a little bit and test them out to see if they’ve got the necessary skillset set to do this.

[00:04:00] But of course, we can’t expect perfection and expect it to all run smoothly right off the bat, and they’ve got to be given training. I see this all the time where someone will test someone out and go, “Yes, I tried him. He was useless at ordering the materials or useless at the takeoffs.” And, I asked the question, “Well what training did you give them?”

“Oh no, I just told them what I wanted done.” Well, that’s not enough. You’re just setting someone up for failure on that. So really you need to log how you want it done. How do you want materials ordered? What is the process that you go through in order to do that? And then you’ve come up with a skilled process and a proper way of doing it . But once you come up with a serious SOP that works, then train them on it, and then if they can’t follow that SOP, then you might have a problem.

That’s the first thing. If you’re worried about inadequate skills or experience, then training could be what gets you over that fear and you could test them out on in that role.

[00:05:00] Another thing that holds business owners back is a concern about favoritism in the company. Or, you get internal politics, so maybe you’ve had two or three people that have been with you a long time and you worry about promoting just one of them because you think, well, if I promote Bob, “Well what’s John going to think about it if I don’t promote him?”

That can be difficult and we don’t want resentment or discord amongst team members. But often you can mitigate this risk if you are honest and transparent with your employees and let them know that you are promoting basing it on meritocracy. So if someone starts to prove themselves, then you are looking to internally promote from within.

What that does then is that that then gives other people in the organization the thought process that actually, maybe I could get promoted, if I up my game a little bit and take a bit more responsibility on and show myself sensible, then maybe I have a chance of also being promoted to this new management position.

[00:06:00] Also a couple of other things you can do is make sure you are having regular appraisals with your team. Sometimes this isn’t done enough with site members, so we might do this with our internal office staff. You may give your a admin person or a bookkeeper an appraisal, but you need to be doing it on site too with those that work with you full-time.

Give them an appraisal, let them know how they’re going. Let them know what targets you want to set for them for the next six months. If we can do that and they’re hitting those targets, then rightly they should be promoted based upon that meritocracy. So think about that if we can make that a culture in the company, then that will help avoid those internal politics and favoritism claims that that may go on.

Another potential reason a business owner might hold back is a resistance to change themselves. They may have a little bit of a mindset problem over this that “everyone’s comfortable in their current roles and I don’t want to mix things up because that’s uncertain, isn’t it? It could cause problems if we start promoting people from within.”

[00:07:00] That really comes down to the business owner’s mindset because, as a business owner, if you are going for growth, then you constantly need to have a culture that’s embracing change and ready to do whatever it takes to grow. A business leader really needs to change their own internal mindset and the mindset of the company so that people can see that change is good.

You’re going to try something out. If it doesn’t work, you can go back to how it used to be or you’re going to try something different, but you certainly don’t want to hold back. Promote in from within, just because you personally are resistant to change, there might be something you need to work on on the inside on that.

There might be a few reasons why a business owner might resist promoting from within and, and how you can overcome them. But let’s just briefly talk about some of the benefits of hiring within, because there are huge benefits from doing that. Rather than bringing someone in from the outside, the first benefit is there is massive employee morale and motivation boosts.

[00:08:00] If they can see that people are being promoted from within, it really sends a strong message that you are going to be be rewarding people for their hard work and that you recognise loyalty and you recognise their commitment, and that’s appreciated. It’s really important to be able to do that and reward people for that attitude.

That will then create an entire environment from throughout the business, not just to the employee that gets promoted, but the entire company will see that and it will improve all sorts across the board from improved job quality, job satisfaction, productivity. All of that will go up if you can improve morale and motivation and certainly promote from within does that.

The second benefit of promoting within is that it maintains your company culture and your values. So when you have people that have been with you a long time, they know how you work. They know what your values are as a company. They know how you treat clients. They know what to do if something goes wrong.

[00:09:00] It’s really important that people in within the business understand what your culture and values are. When people have been with you a long time, they already appreciate all of that. They already understand it, and they may well embody it themselves because they’ve helped create that culture.

That helps, the crucial elements of your business identity, that helps you maintain that if you can promote within and it helps reinforce that a little bit more. That’s another great reason why you should try and promote within.

The third reason is that it saves you a fortune in recruitment costs and onboarding people.

And oftentimes when we think of recruitment costs, we are just thinking of what we pay to either a recruitment company or what our own internal marketing costs us to find someone. But it’s also the time that we need to factor in because it takes a long time to onboard new hires. Then if that new hire doesn’t work out, that’s cost you a fortune. Either in recruitment fees or just in the time that you spent training them and setting them up on all your software and systems.

[00:10:00] When you’ve got someone that’s within you save those resources, you’re not having to pay that money. You still have to train them and you still have to onboard them to their new role, but it’s nowhere near as involved because they already understand the company’s processes and procedures so that comprehensive training isn’t needed as much. That can save you a lot of money and time in the long run.

One of the four things that it can do, is it can help you with your succession planning and your business continuity. Now, you may not be thinking of this yet, it depends what age you are and what age you are listening to this, but at some point you need to think about the business continuity. What happens, If you decide that you want to exit at some point or you want to leave, or what happens if you really go and injure yourself or you get a critical illness and you can’t continue in the business, but you need it to continue for your family’s income or whatever else it’s going to be

[00:11:00] Promoting from within helps you with that succession plan. You’re always making sure that there’s someone ready and capable to take over in those key roles where necessary. That’s really, really important because when you do decide to exit, at some point you may well be able to organise a management buyout.

That could be a great option for you to get the employees of the business to actually buy the business out. That could be done over a period of time. There’s probably a whole other podcast on that, how you could structure a business buyout from management. But it’s a way of you showing that your value in the business continuity and that you want to see it continue after you when you finish the business.

That might not be an initial concern right now, but it may well be 5, 10 years from now and anything can happen, any unforeseen event can happen that may make that plan come about a little bit sooner than what you’re expecting.

So there’s just a few reasons why you want to be promoting from within.

[00:12:00] It’s going to save you a lot of money, it’s really going to boost morale and company culture from within the company, and it’s great for your employees. You can upskill them. If you’re worried about them not having enough ability to be able to do these tasks, you can upskill them, you can train them. Make sure you look from within first, because yes, you might be able to go out and find a great hire out there, and that could be the better option for your business if there’s not someone in your business right now that you can look at then fair enough! But don’t be too hasty to do that. Look from within and see if there’s someone you could train that you might just see a little glint of gold in someone that you think, “Yes, you know what, actually this person might be the one that I could train up”.

Give it a go and I’d love to know your thoughts and how it went.

title.rendered: Building Wealth With Bricks- A Property Portfolio Journey with Danielle Bell Transcript

content.rendered:
Greg Wilkes: 0:42

On today’s podcast, I’m talking to Danielle Bell. Danielle is a great coach and property expert, and I’ve known her for a few years. She’s got her own property portfolio, and if you’ve ever considered getting into property yourself as a construction expert, then you’re going to find this really useful. We’re going to be looking at some of the top tips to ensure that you can make a successful career of property portfolios. Also, we are going to be looking at some of the mistakes that a lot of people make that you can avoid. We’ll be diving into the different types of property deals that you could potentially be doing, so you can decide what route suits you. I hope you get tremendous value from the podcast. Let’s jump in. So, Danielle, awesome to have you on the podcast. I really appreciate you joining us today.

Danielle Bell: 1:28

Thank you so much, Greg. Loving it.

Greg Wilkes: 1:30

Great for you to be here. I know I really wanted to get you on and we’ve been in contact for a while now in the same coaching community. The reason I wanted you on is because I often talk to so many of my clients and builders that are out there, and for most builders their dream is to get into property at some point. They’ve got the skillset to do it, and we see all these programs with everyone doing it. I think as a builder, sometimes you watch these programs like ‘Homes Under the Hammer’ and all those sort of programs, and you think, “I can do this, I can really do this, I can flip these properties or do this and that.” It’s an aim that most have. I think it’s going to be awesome just to talk to you today about some of the things and challenges that people have when they’re trying to build a property portfolio and see what sort of tips we can get over the show .

Danielle Bell: 2:17

Absolutely, brilliant – lets go!

Greg Wilkes: 2:18

Good stuff. Tell us a little bit about yourself, Danielle . How did you get into it? What do you do?

Danielle Bell: 2:23

Ok! So for anyone that’s listening to the podcast, my name’s Danielle Bell. I’m a full-time property investor now and also I’m the founder of ‘Property Sources Made Simple’ which I am claiming as the number one coaching program for property sources in the UK. Hands down . Wasn’t always that way though, Greg, because I come from a financial analysis background, corporate world, it is the cliche story. Corporate girl stuck in the rat race. Worked for the New York Stock Exchange, which when you wrap that up, looks very glamorous, looks super sexy – It was anything but. I was traveling between Belfast, London, Amsterdam, and New York on a weekly basis. We were doing London, then we would do London to Amsterdam, Amsterdam to New York. That was just a loop . Consistently hated everything about it. I really wanted to start a family and that doesn’t quite happen when you’re in two different continents. So I made that decision to leave the corporate world, fell pregnant, fell into property sourcing . It’s really important that I point out Greg, because I think it’s easy to look at something from when you’ve been doing business for a while, I think people can look in and only see the tip of the iceberg and they usually never see what’s going on underneath the surface. It was always a huge dream of mine and my husband’s to get into build a property portfolio. It’s what we knew from our families, it was just kind of what we grew up around separately. But 2008 rocked my parents’ world, in that they lost pretty much everything.

Greg Wilkes: 4:07

Wow.

Danielle Bell: 4:08

Yes… For us it was a case of taking a lot of lessons from 2007/ 2008 and everything that went on thereafter. We had some money set aside to start our first ‘buy to let’, and that was really due to kick off the portfolio while we were working full-time. Very long-story-short, we went through IVF to have our sons . For anybody listen to the podcast will be very aware, IVF is not a cheap process. It is incredibly expensive. That put all our plans to ****

Greg Wilkes: 4:42

That’s your deposit on the ‘buy to let’ gone <laugh>

Danielle Bell: 4:46

Gone! And some, right? It was a crazy journey and I’m very blessed. But when you’ve asked me to say, how did I get started? What’s the background? Look, I was not born with cash to put into this. We weren’t given a leg up. When I really wanted to make a go of this, I was on maternity leave and it was a perfect opportunity to have that little bit of time, that little bit of breathing space. I started to look at things in property that I could capitalise on without having the cash. That’s where property sourcing came into play. And again, for the listeners of your podcast, if you’re not familiar with what property sourcing or property trading is, it’s essentially the art of sourcing good investment deals on behalf of investors, putting it in front of them and they will pay you a fee for going and finding these particular deals. It’s a lucrative strategy, but it’s not get rich quick and that’s totted all over social media (the word) ‘Lucrative’ but you need to be super good at what you do. [Interruption] Sorry, go ahead.

Greg Wilkes: 5:56

(I was just going to say) that’s interesting starting with the sourcing.
